stem: What does an electric circuit mean?
solution:
An electric circuit is a continuous, closed path along which an electric current can flow.

It is made up of a cell or battery (the source of potential difference), connecting wires, a plug key or switch, and one or more electrical components such as a bulb, a resistor or an ammeter. When the key is closed the path is unbroken and current flows; when the key is open the path is broken and the current stops.
groundedIn: §11.1 and Fig. 11.1, the schematic circuit of a cell, bulb, ammeter and plug key.

stem: Define the unit of current.
solution:
The SI unit of electric current is the **ampere (A)**, named after the French scientist Andre-Marie Ampere.

One ampere is the current constituted by the flow of one coulomb of charge per second, that is

\(1\,\text{A} = 1\,\text{C} / 1\,\text{s}\)
groundedIn: §11.1 — 'One ampere is constituted by the flow of one coulomb of charge per second.'

stem: Calculate the number of electrons constituting one coulomb of charge.
solution:
One electron carries a charge of \(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}\).

Number of electrons in one coulomb

\(n = \dfrac{1\,\text{C}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}} = 6.25 \times 10^{18}\)

So about \(6 \times 10^{18}\) electrons make up one coulomb of charge.
groundedIn: §11.1 — one coulomb is 'the charge contained in nearly \(6 \times 10^{18}\) electrons', each of charge \(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C.

stem: Name a device that helps to maintain a potential difference across a conductor.
solution:
A **cell**, or a **battery** made of several cells, maintains a potential difference across a conductor.

The chemical action within a cell generates a potential difference across its terminals even when no current is drawn from it, and the cell expends its stored chemical energy to keep that difference up while current flows.
groundedIn: §11.2 — 'This difference of potential may be produced by a battery, consisting of one or more electric cells.'

stem: What is meant by saying that the potential difference between two points is 1 V?
solution:
Saying that the potential difference between two points is 1 V means that **1 joule of work is done to move a charge of 1 coulomb from one point to the other**.

\(1\,\text{V} = \dfrac{1\,\text{joule}}{1\,\text{coulomb}} = 1\,\text{J}\,\text{C}^{-1}\)
groundedIn: §11.2, Eq. (11.3) — the definition of the volt.

stem: How much energy is given to each coulomb of charge passing through a 6 V battery?
solution:
From \(V = W/Q\), the energy given to a charge \(Q\) is \(W = VQ\).

\(W = 6\,\text{V} \times 1\,\text{C} = 6\,\text{J}\)

So each coulomb of charge passing through a 6 V battery is given 6 joules of energy.

stem: On what factors does the resistance of a conductor depend?
groundedIn: §11.5, Eq. (11.10) — the resistance depends directly on length, inversely on area of cross-section, and on the material; temperature dependence is stated alongside Table 11.2.

stem: Will current flow more easily through a thick wire or a thin wire of the same material, when connected to the same source? Why?
solution:
Current flows more easily through the **thick wire**.

Resistance is inversely proportional to the area of cross-section, \(R = \rho l / A\). A thick wire has a larger area of cross-section, so its resistance is smaller. For the same potential difference, \(I = V/R\) is then larger, so a thick wire carries more current than a thin one of the same material and length.
groundedIn: §11.5, Eq. (11.10), with Ohm's law from §11.4.

stem: Let the resistance of an electrical component remains constant while the potential difference across the two ends of the component decreases to half of its former value. What change will occur in the current through it?
solution:
By Ohm's law \(I = V/R\). With \(R\) constant, the current is directly proportional to the potential difference.

If \(V\) falls to \(V/2\), the new current is

\(I' = \dfrac{V/2}{R} = \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{I}{2}\)

So the current also **falls to half** its former value.
groundedIn: §11.4 Ohm's law — the current is directly proportional to the potential difference at constant temperature.

stem: Why are coils of electric toasters and electric irons made of an alloy rather than a pure metal?
solution:
Two reasons, both of which matter for a heating device:

- **The resistivity of an alloy is generally much higher than that of its constituent metals**, so an alloy coil has a high resistance and produces far more heat for the same current \(\left(H = I^2 Rt\right)\).
- **Alloys do not oxidise, or burn, readily at high temperatures**, so the coil survives being run red-hot again and again.
groundedIn: §11.5 — 'the resistivity of an alloy is generally higher than that of its constituent metals. Alloys do not oxidise (burn) readily at high temperatures. For this reason, they are commonly used in electrical heating devices'; see also Table 11.2.

context: Use the data in Table 11.2 to answer the following –
stem: Which among iron and mercury is a better conductor?
solution:
**Iron** is the better conductor.

From Table 11.2, the resistivity of iron is \(10.0 \times 10^{-8}\,\Omega\,\text{m}\) while that of mercury is \(94.0 \times 10^{-8}\,\Omega\,\text{m}\). The lower the resistivity, the better the conductor, and iron's resistivity is almost ten times smaller.
groundedIn: Table 11.2 — electrical resistivity of some substances at 20°C.

context: Use the data in Table 11.2 to answer the following –
stem: Which material is the best conductor?
solution:
**Silver** is the best conductor.

Its resistivity, \(1.60 \times 10^{-8}\,\Omega\,\text{m}\), is the lowest of every material listed in Table 11.2 — just below copper at \(1.62 \times 10^{-8}\,\Omega\,\text{m}\).
groundedIn: Table 11.2 — electrical resistivity of some substances at 20°C.

stem: Draw a schematic diagram of a circuit consisting of a battery of three cells of 2 V each, a 5 \(\Omega\) resistor, an 8 \(\Omega\) resistor, and a 12 \(\Omega\) resistor, and a plug key, all connected in series.
solution:
Draw a single closed loop, and place around it, in order: the battery, the plug key and the three resistors.

- The **battery** is three cells joined end to end, each drawn as a long line (positive) beside a short thick line (negative), giving a total of \(3 \times 2\,\text{V} = 6\,\text{V}\).
- The **plug key** is drawn as \(-(\bullet)-\) for a closed key.
- The three **resistors**, 5 \(\Omega\), 8 \(\Omega\) and 12 \(\Omega\), are drawn as zig-zag symbols one after another along the loop, so the same current passes through each in turn.

Because they are in series the total resistance is \(5 + 8 + 12 = 25\,\Omega\).

Use the symbols of Table 11.1 and the layout of Fig. 11.6 as the model.
groundedIn: Table 11.1 for the component symbols and Fig. 11.6 for the series layout; §11.6.1 for the series rule.

stem: Redraw the circuit of Question 1, putting in an ammeter to measure the current through the resistors and a voltmeter to measure the potential difference across the 12 \(\Omega\) resistor. What would be the readings in the ammeter and the voltmeter?
solution:
The **ammeter** goes in series, anywhere in the loop, because the same current flows throughout a series circuit. The **voltmeter** goes in parallel, connected across the two ends of the 12 \(\Omega\) resistor alone.

Total resistance \(R_s = 5\,\Omega + 8\,\Omega + 12\,\Omega = 25\,\Omega\).

Total potential difference \(V = 3 \times 2\,\text{V} = 6\,\text{V}\).

Ammeter reading:

\(I = \dfrac{V}{R_s} = \dfrac{6\,\text{V}}{25\,\Omega} = 0.24\,\text{A}\)

Voltmeter reading, across the 12 \(\Omega\) resistor:

\(V_{12} = IR = 0.24\,\text{A} \times 12\,\Omega = 2.88\,\text{V} \approx 2.9\,\text{V}\)
groundedIn: §11.1 (an ammeter is always connected in series) and §11.2 (a voltmeter is always connected in parallel); the arithmetic uses Eq. (11.14) and Ohm's law.

context: Judge the equivalent resistance when the following are connected in parallel –
stem: 1 \(\Omega\) and \(10^6\,\Omega\)
solution:
\(\dfrac{1}{R_p} = \dfrac{1}{1} + \dfrac{1}{10^6} = 1.000001\)

\(R_p \approx 0.999999\,\Omega\), which is **just under 1 \(\Omega\)**.

The point to notice: in a parallel combination the equivalent resistance is always smaller than the smallest resistance present, and a very large resistance in parallel makes almost no difference at all.
groundedIn: §11.6.2, Eq. (11.18) — the reciprocal of the equivalent resistance is the sum of the reciprocals.

context: Judge the equivalent resistance when the following are connected in parallel –
stem: 1 \(\Omega\) and \(10^3\,\Omega\), and \(10^6\,\Omega\)
solution:
\(\dfrac{1}{R_p} = \dfrac{1}{1} + \dfrac{1}{10^3} + \dfrac{1}{10^6} = 1.001001\)

\(R_p \approx 0.999\,\Omega\), again **slightly less than 1 \(\Omega\)**.

The equivalent resistance is dominated by the smallest resistor in the group; the two large ones barely contribute.

stem: An electric lamp of 100 \(\Omega\), a toaster of resistance 50 \(\Omega\), and a water filter of resistance 500 \(\Omega\) are connected in parallel to a 220 V source. What is the resistance of an electric iron connected to the same source that takes as much current as all three appliances, and what is the current through it?
solution:
First find the equivalent resistance of the three appliances in parallel:

\(\dfrac{1}{R_p} = \dfrac{1}{100} + \dfrac{1}{50} + \dfrac{1}{500} = \dfrac{5 + 10 + 1}{500} = \dfrac{16}{500}\)

\(R_p = \dfrac{500}{16} = 31.25\,\Omega\)

The electric iron is to draw the same total current from the same source, so it must have the same resistance:

\(R = 31.25\,\Omega\)

The current through it is

\(I = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{220\,\text{V}}{31.25\,\Omega} = 7.04\,\text{A}\)
groundedIn: §11.6.2, Eq. (11.18), with Ohm's law from §11.4.

stem: What are the advantages of connecting electrical devices in parallel with the battery instead of connecting them in series?
solution:
- **Each device gets the full voltage of the source.** In series the potential difference is shared out, so every device runs below its rating.
- **Each device draws the current it needs.** A series circuit forces the same current through everything, which is impracticable when, say, a bulb and a heater need very different currents.
- **One device failing does not stop the others.** In series, a single broken component breaks the whole circuit and nothing works — which is why a single dead bulb puts out a whole string of fairy lights.
- **The total resistance of the circuit is reduced**, so a larger total current can be drawn.
- Each device can be **switched on and off independently**.
groundedIn: §11.6.2 — the discussion following Example 11.9 on why series circuits are impracticable and how a parallel circuit divides the current.

context: How can three resistors of resistances 2 \(\Omega\), 3 \(\Omega\), and 6 \(\Omega\) be connected to give a total resistance of
stem: 4 \(\Omega\)?
solution:
Connect the **3 \(\Omega\) and 6 \(\Omega\) in parallel**, and put the **2 \(\Omega\) in series** with that combination.

Parallel part:

\(\dfrac{1}{R_p} = \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{2 + 1}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), so \(R_p = 2\,\Omega\)

Total:

\(R = 2\,\Omega + 2\,\Omega = 4\,\Omega\)
groundedIn: §11.6.1 for the series rule Eq. (11.14) and §11.6.2 for the parallel rule Eq. (11.18).

context: How can three resistors of resistances 2 \(\Omega\), 3 \(\Omega\), and 6 \(\Omega\) be connected to give a total resistance of
stem: 1 \(\Omega\)?
solution:
Connect **all three in parallel**.

\(\dfrac{1}{R_p} = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{3 + 2 + 1}{6} = 1\)

\(R_p = 1\,\Omega\)

context: What is (a) the highest, (b) the lowest total resistance that can be secured by combinations of four coils of resistance 4 \(\Omega\), 8 \(\Omega\), 12 \(\Omega\), 24 \(\Omega\)?
stem: The highest total resistance
solution:
The highest total resistance is obtained by connecting **all four coils in series**, because a series combination is greater than any individual resistance:

\(R_s = 4 + 8 + 12 + 24 = 48\,\Omega\)
groundedIn: §11.6.1, Eq. (11.14) — the series combination 'is thus greater than any individual resistance'.

context: What is (a) the highest, (b) the lowest total resistance that can be secured by combinations of four coils of resistance 4 \(\Omega\), 8 \(\Omega\), 12 \(\Omega\), 24 \(\Omega\)?
stem: The lowest total resistance
solution:
The lowest total resistance is obtained by connecting **all four coils in parallel**:

\(\dfrac{1}{R_p} = \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{8} + \dfrac{1}{12} + \dfrac{1}{24} = \dfrac{6 + 3 + 2 + 1}{24} = \dfrac{12}{24} = \dfrac{1}{2}\)

\(R_p = 2\,\Omega\)
groundedIn: §11.6.2, Eq. (11.18) — a parallel combination is smaller than the smallest individual resistance.

stem: Why does the cord of an electric heater not glow while the heating element does?
solution:
The cord and the heating element carry the **same current**, because they are in series. By Joule's law \(H = I^2 Rt\), the heat produced then depends on the resistance.

The heating element is made of an alloy of **high resistivity** and is long and thin, so its resistance is large and a great deal of heat is produced in it — enough to make it glow. The cord is made of copper, whose resistivity is very low, and it is thick, so its resistance is very small and hardly any heat is produced in it. Its temperature stays low and it does not glow.
groundedIn: §11.7, Eq. (11.21) \(H = I^2 Rt\), with the resistivity figures of Table 11.2 and the remarks on alloys in §11.5.

stem: Compute the heat generated while transferring 96000 coulomb of charge in one hour through a potential difference of 50 V.
solution:
The work done in moving a charge \(Q\) through a potential difference \(V\) is \(W = VQ\), and that energy appears as heat:

\(H = VQ = 50\,\text{V} \times 96000\,\text{C}\)

\(H = 4.8 \times 10^{6}\,\text{J}\)

The time of one hour is not needed for the heat itself — it would only be needed to work out the power.
groundedIn: §11.7 — the source supplies energy \(VQ\), and in a purely resistive circuit it is all dissipated as heat; Eq. (11.20) \(H = VIt\).

stem: An electric iron of resistance 20 \(\Omega\) takes a current of 5 A. Calculate the heat developed in 30 s.
solution:
By Joule's law of heating,

\(H = I^2 Rt\)

\(= (5\,\text{A})^2 \times 20\,\Omega \times 30\,\text{s}\)

\(= 25 \times 20 \times 30\)

\(= 15000\,\text{J} = 1.5 \times 10^{4}\,\text{J}\)
groundedIn: §11.7, Eq. (11.21) \(H = I^2 Rt\) — Joule's law of heating.

stem: What determines the rate at which energy is delivered by a current?
solution:
The rate at which energy is delivered by a current is the **electric power**, and it is determined by the potential difference across the device and the current through it:

\(P = VI = I^2 R = \dfrac{V^2}{R}\)

So for a given appliance it is fixed by the supply voltage and the appliance's own resistance.
groundedIn: §11.8, Eq. (11.22) — 'the rate of consumption of energy' is the electric power.

stem: An electric motor takes 5 A from a 220 V line. Determine the power of the motor and the energy consumed in 2 h.
solution:
Power:

\(P = VI = 220\,\text{V} \times 5\,\text{A} = 1100\,\text{W} = 1.1\,\text{kW}\)

Energy consumed in 2 hours:

\(E = P \times t = 1.1\,\text{kW} \times 2\,\text{h} = 2.2\,\text{kW h}\)

In joules, \(2.2\,\text{kW h} = 2.2 \times 3.6 \times 10^{6}\,\text{J} = 7.92 \times 10^{6}\,\text{J}\).
groundedIn: §11.8, Eq. (11.22) \(P = VI\) and the definition of the kilowatt hour, \(1\,\text{kW h} = 3.6 \times 10^6\,\text{J}\).
